Everyone and every thing should sing praises to Yahweh because he is worthy of all praise.
chapters.99:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 99 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Yahweh reigns over all peoples (1–3)
2. Yahweh loves justice and rules rightly (4–5)
3. Yahweh answers his faithful servants (6–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s justice

God is just and fair. Moses, Aaron and Samuel each prayed to him and obeyed him, and he answered their prayers.
chapters.100:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 100 is the last of this group of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100).

1. Call to joyful praise (1–2)
2. Reason for worship: Yahweh is God (3)
3. Enter with thanksgiving and praise (4)
4. Yahweh’s character is the foundation of praise (5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s care for his creation

God made mankind and takes good care of people.
chapters.101:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 101 is a psalm of David asking God’s help to live as a person should. With God’s help, David pledges to rule uprightly and to get rid of all evildoers.

1. David commits to upright life (1–2)
2. David rejects evil and deceit (3–7)
3. David promises justice and faithfulness (8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Encouragement

David wanted to encourage all the good people in the land and restrain all the evil people.
chapters.102:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 102 is a “lament.”

1. Cry of distress and plea for mercy (1–11)
2. Confidence in Yahweh’s eternal purposes and mercy (12–17)
3. Call to record and remember Yahweh’s mercies (18–22)
4. Yahweh sustains and remains unchanging (23–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Salvation

The psalmist does not want to die young. He also wants to see Jerusalem saved.
chapters.103:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 103 is the first in a series of five “psalm of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107).

1. Call to bless Yahweh with whole being (1–2)
2. Yahweh’s forgiveness, healing, and provision (3–5)
3. Yahweh’s compassionate character (6–14)
4. Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness from everlasting (15–22)
5. Yahweh’s sovereign rule over all (19–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s grace

God shows his goodness to us by forgiving our sins and not punishing us as much as we deserve.
chapters.104:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 104 is the second in the series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107).

1. Yahweh’s greatness in creation (1–6)
2. Yahweh’s sustaining care over creation (7–30)
3. Yahweh’s glory declared forever (31–32)
4. Everlasting praise to Yahweh (33–35)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s creation

God has created everything good on earth, in the sky, and in the sea.
chapters.105:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 105 is the third in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107). Psalm 105 retells the history of Israel from Yahweh’s covenant with Abraham, to the people’s enslavement in Egypt, to Yahweh’s liberation of the people through the plagues in Egypt, to Yahweh giving them the land of Canaan.

1. Praise Yahweh and seek his works (1–6)
2. Yahweh’s covenant and deeds with the patriarchs (7–15)
3. Yahweh’s guidance over Joseph and Israel in Egypt (16–25)
4. Yahweh’s deliverance and provision in the wilderness (26–45)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s protection

God protected Abraham and Jacob. He worked throughout Israel’s history to bring Israel into the land he had promised them.
chapters.106:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 106 is the fourth in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107). The book of Psalms is divided into five sections, also called “books,” and Psalm 106 ends book four. Verses 47 and 48 are considered to be a closing petition and praise for book four, rather than belonging specifically to Psalm 106.

1. Praise Yahweh for his goodness and faithfulness (1–3)
2. Plea for pardon and Yahweh’s acceptance (4–6)
3. Recount Israel’s rebellion and Yahweh’s mercy (7–46)
4. Prayer and praise to Yahweh (47–48)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Israel’s sin

Although Israel continually sinned in the desert, God still took them to the Promised Land.
chapters.107:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 107 is the last in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107).

1. A call to thanksgiving (1–3)
2. Stories of Yahweh’s deliverance (4–32)
3. Yahweh’s transformative power (33–41)
4. A final exhortation (42–43)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

The psalmist praises Yahweh for saving people lost in the desert, in prison, sick, in a storm at sea, homeless and oppressed.
chapters.108:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 108 is a psalm of praise and petition.

1. Praise for Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness (1–5)
2. Yahweh’s sovereign dominion and promised kingdom (6–9)
3. Prayer for deliverance and victory (10–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Victory

God affirms that he is in control of all nations, but the psalmist has not had success against his enemies. He admits that only God can give him victory, and so he asks God to give him victory over Edom.
chapters.109:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 109 is a “psalm of petition,” asking Yahweh to give David relief from his enemies who are falsely accusing him and persecuting him. He also asks Yahweh to curse these people who are enemies of both Yahweh and David.

1. Complaint and accusation (1–5)
2. Curses against enemies (6–20)
3. David’s plea for himself (21–29)
4. Praise and confidence (30–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Cursing of Enemies

In this psalm, David takes evil very seriously and calls on Yahweh to punish those who are doing evil to himself and others so that the evil will stop. It is important to note that David does not take vengeance personally, but only calls on Yahweh to combat evil and to perform justice, as Yahweh has promised to do.
chapters.110:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 110 is a psalm honoring the king as he becomes king and was also recognized as a prophecy about the coming messiah.

1. The divine proclamation (1–2)
2. The people’s response (3)
3. The eternal priesthood (4)
4. The king’s judgment & victory (5–7)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### King

Yahweh will enable the king to conquer his enemies. Christ is seen as both high priest and king.
chapters.111:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 111 is a psalm of praise to God for his miracles and care.

1. Call to praise (1–2)
2. Yahweh’s majestic works (3–6)
3. Yahweh’s trustworthy and enduring nature (7–9)
4. Wisdom and praise (10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s character

God is great. He has given his people food, land, and always keeps his promises to his people.
chapters.112:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 112 is a “wisdom psalm” teaching the value of a righteous life.

1. The blessings of the Yahweh-fearing (1–3)
2. The character and security of the upright (4–9)
3. The contrast with the wicked (10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Righteous people

The righteous people will be well-known for their generosity and they will not have to worry about bad news because God is taking care of them.
chapters.113:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 113 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his goodness.

1. The call to universal and eternal praise (1–3)
2. The greatness of Yahweh’s majesty (4–6)
3. The grace of Yahweh’s compassion (7–9)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s help

God helps the poor and gives children to the wife who cannot conceive children.
chapters.114:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 114 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his miracles in bringing the people of Israel to the promised land.

1. God claims his people (1–2)
2. Creation’s astonished response (3–6)
3. Earth’s reverent awe (7–8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

The psalmist praises God for all the ways he helped his people in the past. This psalm references many miraculous events the Israelites experienced like the parting of the Sea of Reeds (Red Sea), the reversal of the Jordan River, bringing water from a rock, and the awe-inspiring presence of God at Mount Sinai, with creation itself responding, as the earth trembled with, God’s power as he delivered his people from Egypt and led them to the land he had promised them.
chapters.115:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 115 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Glory belongs to Yahweh alone (1–3)
2. Futility of idols (4–8)
3. Call for God’s people to trust Yahweh (9–11)
4. Yahweh’s Faithfulness and Blessing (12–15)
5. Life, praise, and hope in the living God (16–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is in heaven and is able to do whatever he wants. Idols can not do anything. Therefore, people and priests should trust Yahweh for their protection.
chapters.116:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 116 is a “psalm of praise” for saving the psalmist’s life.

1. Declaration of love and prayer (1–2)
2. Recounting deliverance and finding rest (3–9)
3. Vows, sacrifice, and public praise (10–19)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Healing

The psalmist was very sick and expected to die but God healed him. So he will pay his vow and sacrifice an offering of thanks.
chapters.117:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 117 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Call to praise
2. Reasons to praise

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Praise

Everyone should praise God for his love and unending faithfulness.
chapters.118:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 118 is a “psalm of thanksgiving” written on the occasion of a military victory. At the same time, it is a messianic psalm that looks forward to the triumph of Jesus Christ. Jesus applied Psalm 118:22 to himself (Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17), and the apostle Peter applied it to Jesus both in a speech recorded in Acts (Acts 4:11), and in his first letter (1 Peter 2:7). See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to Thanksgiving (1–4)
2. Testimony of deliverance (5–18)
3. Messianic celebration (9–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Rejected stone

The psalmist praised Yahweh for rescuing him. God enabled him to overpower his enemies. The new Testament, and even Jesus himself, saw the rejected stone as a reference to the Messiah’s rejection by the Jewish leaders.
chapters.119:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 119 is a “wisdom psalm” about the law of Yahweh. This psalm is an “acrostic” (see discussion in the Introduction to Psalms), an alphabetic poem with twenty-two groups of eight verses each. Each group begins with a letter of the alphabet in the order of the Hebrew alphabet.

The psalmist uses many different words to refer to Yahweh’s message to us. You could attempt to use a different word for each term (ULT uses words such as “precepts,” “commandments,” and “law”), but most languages will not have that many, so just use the words that your language has.

1. Blessing for those who walk in Yahweh’s law (1–32)
2. Prayer for understanding and guidance from Yahweh’s word (33–72)
3. Comfort and hope in Yahweh’s word during affliction (73–112)
4. Devotion to Yahweh’s law despite opposition (113–144)
5. Cry for deliverance and life through Yahweh’s word (145–176)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### The law

The psalmist loved the law of Yahweh and was blessed by obeying it.

## “your word”

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist uses the phrase “your word” to refer more generally to Yahweh’s commandments, instructions, promises, and messages to us.

## Request form

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

2. Judgment on the deceiver (3–4)
3. Complaint of distant dwelling (5–7)

Psalm 122 one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). ## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 123 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). ## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm

### Trust

Just as a servant trusts his master to protect him, so the psalmist is trusting God to stop proud people from insulting him.
chapters.124:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 124 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

chapters.125:
## Structure and Formatting

Psalm 125 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. This song is also a “psalm of trust,” expressing communal confidence that Yahweh protects his people as permanently as mountains surround Jerusalem.
